classification_signals: Abstract: 'This research addresses the possibility of using the perception of building materials as a tool for upgrading the architecture.'
Abstract: 'The first theme handles the theoretical background of perception... The second theme addresses the building material...'

Section 1.3 Approach: 'For reaching the research's objective, the study addresses following points: -Basic conceptions of perception process... -Considering the building material and factors affecting its selection... -Considering and analyzing examples of building materials...'

Section 6. PERCEPTION LEVELS OF MATERIAL IN ARCHITECTURE: 'It is clear from the analytical study that the technologies play an essential role in proposing the re-classification of perception levels to the following:' (followed by definitions of Form, Functional, Interactive, Virtual, Non-Perception levels).

The paper synthesizes existing knowledge and analyzes various architectural examples (Section 5) to build a new conceptual model (Section 6), rather than presenting new empirical data or a systematic review.
title: PERCEPTION OF BUILDING MATERIALS IN ARCHITECTURE

limitations: The paper does not explicitly state its own limitations. However, it notes that a design suggesting clay but built with concrete faced criticism because the suggestion differed from constructional reality due to 'weakness of skills and available possibilities that did not enable the designer to execute the idea' (p. 13), implying practical limitations in achieving desired perceptions.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper explores how the perception of building materials can enhance architectural design. It examines the theoretical underpinnings of perception, impression, and stereotype, and analyzes various building materials—natural, mixed, and fabricated—along with technologies like smart materials and nanotechnology that alter their properties and perception. Through an analytical study of architectural examples, the research proposes a new classification of material perception levels: Form, Functional, Interactive, Virtual, and Non-Perception. The paper concludes that understanding these perception levels is crucial for selecting materials that align with design objectives and create successful architectural experiences, advocating for a new standard in material selection beyond mere cost or strength. The paper does not explicitly state its own limitations.
